transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I... well, I suppose what brings me in is that things have become quite impossible to manage day-to-day. You see, I live in this wonderful older apartment—I've been there for years, ever since I stopped working, and it has these very thick, sturdy walls. But lately, despite the architecture, I keep hearing these voices. Very, very clear voices. 

It’s... it’s women, mostly. They whisper right from behind the walls of my apartment. At first, I thought it was a draft, or maybe the plumbing, but no, it is distinct talking. And it isn't just at home, either, which is what really pushed me to come in. I like to go to the art museums downtown, usually during the week when it's deserted and I can have some peace to look at the exhibits. But I'll be standing in a completely empty gallery, completely alone, not a security guard in sight, and I'll hear them there, too. Whispering from behind the museum walls. 

They talk to me about the archives. They tell me exactly which photographs belong in the archive, sorting through them, deciding what needs to be preserved and what doesn't. It’s so vivid, and they just won't stop whispering about the photographs. I try to listen, because it feels incredibly important, this curation they are doing, but it’s just constantly happening, and I don't know how they're getting into the walls of both my home and the museum... it's just exhausting, frankly.
When these voices whisper to you about the photographs and the archive, do they ever command you to do something, or do they just describe and comment on what should be done?

Well, it’s... it’s not exactly an order, if that’s what you mean. They aren't barking commands at me like a drill sergeant or telling me to go out and do things, no. Like I was saying before, it's just these incredibly clear voices—these women—whispering right through the plaster and the drywall of my apartment, and of course, echoing from behind the walls in those completely empty museum rooms. 

It's more of a... a relentless running commentary. They are just so entirely focused on telling me which photographs belong in the archive. They discuss it with such absolute authority, you know? They'll describe the exact photograph they are looking at, down to the tiniest, most specific details—the shading, the contrast, whether it's a silver gelatin print, the way the subjects in the picture are standing or looking away from the camera—and then they just state, very matter-of-factly, whether it makes the cut for the archive or if it has to be discarded. 

It’s a constant, endless sorting process. "This one belongs, that one doesn't. This one has water damage, it cannot go in." Over and over and over. So they aren't telling *me* to go physically move the pictures or commanding me to act, but they are just constantly describing what should be done with them, narrating this whole grand curation process from behind the walls. And because it's so vivid, and they just never, ever stop talking about the archive, I end up feeling this immense pressure, like I'm supposed to be participating somehow, even though they're just commenting. It's just... it's every single detail of every single photograph they are sorting, and I can't get away from the sound of it.

Before these voices started, or around the time they began, did you experience any period where your mood was significantly elevated—feeling unusually energetic, needing less sleep, or having racing thoughts—or conversely, a period of deep depression or hopelessness?

Well, it's... it's interesting you ask about that, because yes, there are these periods, these distinct stretches of time. It's not just the voices, you see. Before the whispering became so constant, and even sometimes while it's happening, I get these days... well, "days" doesn't really capture it. I get these stretches where I feel absolutely radiant. It's this glowing, humming feeling right in the center of my chest, like I've been plugged into a socket, and I feel so completely chosen. It's as if the universe has pulled back the curtain just for me, and I have this immense, sparkling clarity about everything. I'll have these grand, beautiful plans, just bursting with energy, and I feel like I could walk for miles, or catalog the entire history of the world all by myself. 

But the problem—and this is what makes it so incredibly difficult to manage—is that if anyone, and I mean anyone, dares to interrupt me during these times... if someone at the grocery store looks at me the wrong way, or if a neighbor questions what I'm doing, or if someone tells me I need to slow down or get some rest... I become furious. Just absolutely, blindingly enraged. It's not just annoyance, Doctor, it's a fury that burns right through me. It feels as if they aren't just disagreeing with me, but as if they are actively trying to erase me. Like they are trying to snuff out this radiant light I've been given. I'll snap at people, I'll yell... I can't even control it because it feels so deeply personal, like a threat to my very existence. So yes, there are those times of feeling so elevated and chosen, but it flips so quickly into this terrible, defensive anger if anyone gets in my way.

You've described these periods where you feel radiant and energetic, and then very angry if interrupted. Do you also experience distinct periods where your mood goes in the opposite direction—times when you feel deeply sad, hopeless, or depressed, with low energy and little interest in things?

Well, yes... yes, I do. It’s... it's like a pendulum, I suppose, but a very heavy, dragging pendulum. After those periods of being so bright and so full of fire, there are these other times. Long, long stretches, really. And it's not just feeling a little down, Doctor, it's this profound emptiness. I have this lovely little kitchen table by a window, and I used to keep all these potted herbs there—basil, thyme, rosemary—I'd tend to them every morning, making sure they had just the right amount of water and sunlight. But during these... these other times, I just sit there. I'll sit at that kitchen table for hours, just staring, and I watch the soil turn to dust and the leaves shrivel up and turn brown, and I just don't care. I don't have the energy to even lift a watering can. 

The phone will ring—friends leaving messages, checking in, inviting me out. I used to love going out. A friend will leave a voicemail asking if I want to go to a symphony concert, or there will be an invitation to a new gallery opening downtown, which, as I mentioned, I usually adore... but I just listen to the machine click off. I don't call them back. I don't feel even a flicker of interest. It's as if all the color has been completely drained out of the world, and there’s just nothing left but this heavy, gray stillness. I just sit there with the dead plants, feeling completely disconnected from everything and everyone, and it goes on for weeks like that, just this terrible, dragging weight where nothing matters at all.

When you're not in one of those elevated, radiant periods and not in one of those deeply depressed, empty periods—when your mood feels more normal or neutral—do you still hear those voices whispering about the photographs and the archive?

Well, yes... yes, I do. And that is exactly what makes it all so incredibly exhausting, if I’m being completely honest with you. You’d think that if the pendulum stopped swinging—if I wasn't feeling so grand and radiant, or if I wasn't sinking into that terrible, heavy grayness—that the rest of it would stop, too. But it doesn't. 

There was a period just recently, actually, a stretch of several weeks where I felt... well, just ordinary. I wasn't especially energized, I wasn't feeling grand or chosen by the universe, and I wasn't depressed either. I was just waking up, making my Earl Grey tea, reading the morning paper... just going about a perfectly normal routine, sleeping a normal amount. But even then, even when my mood was completely level and fine, the whispers were still there. Every single day. I would be standing in the kitchen, feeling perfectly calm, and I'd still hear them murmuring through the drywall, going on and on about the archive and the photographs. 

And it wasn't just the voices in the apartment, either. During those exact same weeks, when I wasn't having any of those extreme moods, I remained absolutely convinced that the arts people—the curators and the museum board members—were monitoring my phone. I was certain of it. I would look at the telephone sitting there on the hall table, and I just knew they were listening in on my line, tracking who I was talking to, making sure I wasn't going to interfere with their sorting process. I could practically feel them listening through the receiver. I even started wrapping the phone in a thick wool scarf and putting it inside a drawer just to muffle it, because I knew they were there. So, yes, for weeks at a time, even without the fire or the emptiness, the voices and the monitoring... they just keep right on going.

When you first started hearing these voices whispering about the photographs and the archive, was that happening during one of those times when you were feeling especially radiant and energetic, or did the voices begin at a different time—perhaps when your mood was more normal, or during one of those heavy, depressed periods?

Oh, let me think back to when it all really began... because it is quite a vivid memory, actually. It was absolutely during one of those times when I felt like I had electricity just... just humming through my veins. Yes, the radiant periods. I remember it so clearly because I was barely sleeping at all. Maybe two, three hours a night, if that? But I didn't need sleep, Doctor. I would wake up at two in the morning, the house would be completely dark, and I just had to get straight to work. 

I was racing, just practically flying from one archive task to another. I had all these boxes of photographs—thousands of them, really—spread out all over the living room floor, the dining table, even down the hallway. I was categorizing them by the angle of the shadows in the background, cross-referencing them, making these incredibly intricate piles... and it was right then, right in the middle of all that frantic, beautiful work, that the whispering started. 

While I was rushing around, moving stacks of photos and making notes, I was also hearing those women’s voices. They would murmur just behind the plaster, almost keeping pace with me as I worked. And at the exact same time, I started feeling absolutely certain that the museum board was tracking my work. I just knew they were monitoring how quickly I was sorting the archive. I could feel their presence, like they were keeping a ledger of every single photograph I categorized. I figured they had to be tracking me because my methodology was so important, you see, and they needed to make sure I was doing it exactly to their hidden specifications. 

So, yes, to answer your question, the women's voices and that absolute certainty about the board tracking me... they started right in the thick of that period when I was sleeping only a few hours and rushing from one archive pile to the next. It was all happening at once, intertwined—I couldn't stop working, and they wouldn't stop whispering.

During those several weeks when your mood felt completely normal and stable—when you were just having your Earl Grey tea and reading the paper—how long had the voices about the archive been going on at that point? Had they been present continuously since they first started during that energetic period, or did they stop at some point and then come back?

Well, that’s the truly exhausting part of it all, Doctor. They haven't stopped. Not once. You would think—and I certainly hoped—that they might take a holiday, or perhaps that the museum board would find some other archivist to bother for a little while, but no. It has been a constant, uninterrupted stream. 

If I trace it all the way back to that first night when I was down on the floor with all those photographs, feeling so electric and alive... well, I remember I was wearing my heavy wool cardigan, the burgundy one with the tortoiseshell buttons, because there was still quite a chill in the air. And so, if I count the months... it has been about eight months now. Yes, eight entire months of this. 

And in all that time, whether I was flying high and barely sleeping, or sitting in that terrible, heavy gray stillness watching my poor potted herbs turn to dust, or even just having that perfectly ordinary cup of Earl Grey tea on a Tuesday morning... the voices and that absolute certainty that people are watching my archive have been right there with me. Every single day for eight months. 

I kept thinking, surely, when the seasons change, the acoustics in the apartment will shift and the murmuring in the drywall will fade. I remember in April, when the spring rain started, I thought the sound of the rain against the windowpanes might drown them out, or that the board members monitoring my telephone would finally get bored of tracking my methodology and move on to someone else's collection. But they didn't. May came and went, June, July... and the whispering just kept right on going, steady as a metronome. It’s a terribly long time to be observed so closely, Doctor. Eight months of never truly being alone in your own home, having to wrap the telephone in a scarf and hide it in a drawer just to try and get a single moment's peace... it really does wear a person down, you know? Just the sheer endurance it takes to listen to them for eight months straight...

During those long stretches when you were in that heavy, gray, depressed state—sitting with the dead plants, feeling completely disconnected—were the voices whispering about the archive still just as loud and constant as they were when you were feeling radiant and energetic, or did they quiet down or change in some way during those depressed periods?

Well... gosh, that is a very particular question, isn't it? When I am in that terrible, sinking grayness... it's so hard to explain how time works, or how sound works, for that matter. You mentioned the plants, and it's true, I would just sit in my green velvet armchair for hours upon hours, just watching the leaves crisp up and fall onto the rug. I didn't even have the energy to sweep them up, they just lay there turning to dust. The whole apartment felt like it was submerged underwater, or like my head was wrapped in this thick, heavy cotton batting. 

So, as for whether the voices were just as loud, or if they changed in some way... I honestly don't know. I really couldn't tell you. I mean, I didn't notice a specific change in their volume or their tone, but I also wasn't exactly in a state to measure it, you see? 

When you're feeling that completely empty, when just the thought of walking to the kitchen sink for a glass of water feels like you're trying to climb a mountain in a snowstorm, your perception of everything gets so terribly muddled. Were they louder? Were they quieter? Did they change their cadence? I'm simply not sure. I just know they didn't leave. They were still there in the walls, still murmuring about the archive and the museum board, but whether the pitch or the volume shifted... it's all just a heavy blur to me. 

It's a bit like asking if the rain sounds different against the glass when you're weeping, you know? You don't analyze the acoustics, you just know that it's still raining. So, no, I really couldn't say if they quieted down or got louder. I just didn't have the mental capacity to notice those kinds of fine details when I was feeling so utterly disconnected from the rest of the world. I just knew I was trapped in that chair, and they were still talking.

When you're feeling that heavy, gray emptiness and sitting in your armchair—during those deeply depressed periods—are you still absolutely convinced that the museum board is monitoring your telephone and tracking your work, or does that certainty fade away even though the voices might still be there?

Oh, it doesn't fade. No, not in the slightest, Doctor. Even when I am sitting there, feeling like I have lead weights in my pockets and I can barely lift my head off the velvet cushion of that armchair... the certainty doesn't go anywhere. Because, you see, the facts don't change just because my mood has plummeted and I'm too exhausted to move. 

I am completely, absolutely convinced that the museum board—and, actually, the city arts people as well, they are definitely involved now—they have been monitoring my phone this entire time. Even when I'm not making calls! I sit there in the terrible grayness, staring at the drawer where I've wrapped the receiver in my scarves, and I know they're on the other end, just waiting, listening to the silence in my apartment. 

And why wouldn't they? They know exactly what I have sitting in those boxes. My Caribbean archive... it is so incredibly significant, Doctor. The way I've cataloged the photographs, the history from the islands, it is going to completely change how the galleries tell the truth. It will upend their entire curated narrative, and they are absolutely terrified of that. The city arts people are desperate to control the history, you see, to keep things exactly as they are. 

So, no, the conviction never leaves me. Not for a single second. People might try to dismiss it, but no one—absolutely no one—has shown me anything that proves otherwise. Not a single person has been able to give me a shred of evidence that my phone isn't tapped or that my archive isn't being watched. So I just sit there in the heavy stillness, watching the dead leaves on the rug, knowing that the moment I pick up that phone or touch a photograph from the Caribbean collection, they are logging it. You just can't turn off that kind of knowing, Doctor, no matter how terribly depressed you feel. It's exhausting, it really is, having to carry the immense weight of that truth while also feeling like you're drowning in a gray ocean... it just never stops.

Well, yes... yes, I do. It’s... it's like a pendulum, I suppose, but a very heavy, dragging pendulum. After those periods of being so bright and so full of fire, there are these other times. Long, long stretches, really. And it's not just feeling a little down, Doctor, it's this profound emptiness. I have this lovely little kitchen table by a window, and I used to keep all these potted herbs there—basil, thyme, rosemary—I'd tend to them every morning, making sure they had just the right amount of water and sunlight. But during these... these other times, I just sit there. I'll sit at that kitchen table for hours, just staring, and I watch the soil turn to dust and the leaves shrivel up and turn brown, and I just don't care. I don't have the energy to even lift a watering can. 

The phone will ring—friends leaving messages, checking in, inviting me out. I used to love going out. A friend will leave a voicemail asking if I want to go to a symphony concert, or there will be an invitation to a new gallery opening downtown, which, as I mentioned, I usually adore... but I just listen to the machine click off. I don't call them back. I don't feel even a flicker of interest. It's as if all the color has been completely drained out of the world, and there’s just nothing left but this heavy, gray stillness. I just sit there with the dead plants, feeling completely disconnected from everything and everyone, and it goes on for weeks like that, just this terrible, dragging weight where nothing matters at all.

doctor.intent: Determine whether psychotic symptoms (voices) occur exclusively during mood episodes (schizoaffective disorder) or persist during euthymic periods (schizophrenia), which is the key diagnostic distinction between F25.0 and F25.1
doctor.question: When you're not in one of those elevated, radiant periods and not in one of those deeply depressed, empty periods—when your mood feels more normal or neutral—do you still hear those voices whispering about the photographs and the archive?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 3
target_item.manifestation: There was a period of several weeks when I was not especially energized or grand, but I still heard whispers in the apartment and remained convinced the arts people were monitoring my phone.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the hallucinations (hearing voices) occur during periods when my mood is normal or neutral, which directly assesses if psychotic symptoms are present in the absence of a major mood episode.

patient.answer:
Well, yes... yes, I do. And that is exactly what makes it all so incredibly exhausting, if I’m being completely honest with you. You’d think that if the pendulum stopped swinging—if I wasn't feeling so grand and radiant, or if I wasn't sinking into that terrible, heavy grayness—that the rest of it would stop, too. But it doesn't. 

There was a period just recently, actually, a stretch of several weeks where I felt... well, just ordinary. I wasn't especially energized, I wasn't feeling grand or chosen by the universe, and I wasn't depressed either. I was just waking up, making my Earl Grey tea, reading the morning paper... just going about a perfectly normal routine, sleeping a normal amount. But even then, even when my mood was completely level and fine, the whispers were still there. Every single day. I would be standing in the kitchen, feeling perfectly calm, and I'd still hear them murmuring through the drywall, going on and on about the archive and the photographs. 

And it wasn't just the voices in the apartment, either. During those exact same weeks, when I wasn't having any of those extreme moods, I remained absolutely convinced that the arts people—the curators and the museum board members—were monitoring my phone. I was certain of it. I would look at the telephone sitting there on the hall table, and I just knew they were listening in on my line, tracking who I was talking to, making sure I wasn't going to interfere with their sorting process. I could practically feel them listening through the receiver. I even started wrapping the phone in a thick wool scarf and putting it inside a drawer just to muffle it, because I knew they were there. So, yes, for weeks at a time, even without the fire or the emptiness, the voices and the monitoring... they just keep right on going.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms (voices and delusions) began during a mood episode or emerged independently during a period of normal mood, which would help distinguish between schizoaffective disorder (psychosis tied to mood episodes) and schizophrenia (psychosis independent of mood).
doctor.question: When you first started hearing these voices whispering about the photographs and the archive, was that happening during one of those times when you were feeling especially radiant and energetic, or did the voices begin at a different time—perhaps when your mood was more normal, or during one of those heavy, depressed periods?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: During the periods when I was sleeping only a few hours and racing from one archive task to another, I was also hearing the women’s voices and feeling certain the museum board was tracking my work.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the hallucinations (voices) occurred at the same time as the manic symptoms (feeling radiant and energetic), which corresponds to the concurrent presence of psychotic symptoms and a manic episode.

patient.answer:
Oh, let me think back to when it all really began... because it is quite a vivid memory, actually. It was absolutely during one of those times when I felt like I had electricity just... just humming through my veins. Yes, the radiant periods. I remember it so clearly because I was barely sleeping at all. Maybe two, three hours a night, if that? But I didn't need sleep, Doctor. I would wake up at two in the morning, the house would be completely dark, and I just had to get straight to work. 

I was racing, just practically flying from one archive task to another. I had all these boxes of photographs—thousands of them, really—spread out all over the living room floor, the dining table, even down the hallway. I was categorizing them by the angle of the shadows in the background, cross-referencing them, making these incredibly intricate piles... and it was right then, right in the middle of all that frantic, beautiful work, that the whispering started. 

While I was rushing around, moving stacks of photos and making notes, I was also hearing those women’s voices. They would murmur just behind the plaster, almost keeping pace with me as I worked. And at the exact same time, I started feeling absolutely certain that the museum board was tracking my work. I just knew they were monitoring how quickly I was sorting the archive. I could feel their presence, like they were keeping a ledger of every single photograph I categorized. I figured they had to be tracking me because my methodology was so important, you see, and they needed to make sure I was doing it exactly to their hidden specifications. 

So, yes, to answer your question, the women's voices and that absolute certainty about the board tracking me... they started right in the thick of that period when I was sleeping only a few hours and rushing from one archive pile to the next. It was all happening at once, intertwined—I couldn't stop working, and they wouldn't stop whispering.

Had they been present continuously since they first started during that energetic period, or did they stop at some point and then come back?

target_item.name: Psychotic Symptoms Duration
target_item.manifestation: The voices and the certainty that people are watching my archive have been present for about 8 months now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about how long the voices and delusions have been present and whether they have been continuous, which corresponds to the duration of the psychotic symptoms.

patient.answer:
Well, that’s the truly exhausting part of it all, Doctor. They haven't stopped. Not once. You would think—and I certainly hoped—that they might take a holiday, or perhaps that the museum board would find some other archivist to bother for a little while, but no. It has been a constant, uninterrupted stream. 

If I trace it all the way back to that first night when I was down on the floor with all those photographs, feeling so electric and alive... well, I remember I was wearing my heavy wool cardigan, the burgundy one with the tortoiseshell buttons, because there was still quite a chill in the air. And so, if I count the months... it has been about eight months now. Yes, eight entire months of this. 

And in all that time, whether I was flying high and barely sleeping, or sitting in that terrible, heavy gray stillness watching my poor potted herbs turn to dust, or even just having that perfectly ordinary cup of Earl Grey tea on a Tuesday morning... the voices and that absolute certainty that people are watching my archive have been right there with me. Every single day for eight months. 

I kept thinking, surely, when the seasons change, the acoustics in the apartment will shift and the murmuring in the drywall will fade. I remember in April, when the spring rain started, I thought the sound of the rain against the windowpanes might drown them out, or that the board members monitoring my telephone would finally get bored of tracking my methodology and move on to someone else's collection. But they didn't. May came and went, June, July... and the whispering just kept right on going, steady as a metronome. It’s a terribly long time to be observed so closely, Doctor. Eight months of never truly being alone in your own home, having to wrap the telephone in a scarf and hide it in a drawer just to try and get a single moment's peace... it really does wear a person down, you know? Just the sheer endurance it takes to listen to them for eight months straight...

doctor.intent: Determine whether the psychotic symptoms (voices and delusions) persist during depressive episodes at the same intensity/frequency as during manic/elevated episodes, which would help differentiate between Schizoaffective Disorder Bipolar Type (F25.0) where psychosis is independent of mood, versus Bipolar Disorder with mood-congruent psychosis.
doctor.question: During those long stretches when you were in that heavy, gray, depressed state—sitting with the dead plants, feeling completely disconnected—were the voices whispering about the archive still just as loud and constant as they were when you were feeling radiant and energetic, or did they quiet down or change in some way during those depressed periods?

patient.answer:
Well... gosh, that is a very particular question, isn't it? When I am in that terrible, sinking grayness... it's so hard to explain how time works, or how sound works, for that matter. You mentioned the plants, and it's true, I would just sit in my green velvet armchair for hours upon hours, just watching the leaves crisp up and fall onto the rug. I didn't even have the energy to sweep them up, they just lay there turning to dust. The whole apartment felt like it was submerged underwater, or like my head was wrapped in this thick, heavy cotton batting. 

So, as for whether the voices were just as loud, or if they changed in some way... I honestly don't know. I really couldn't tell you. I mean, I didn't notice a specific change in their volume or their tone, but I also wasn't exactly in a state to measure it, you see? 

When you're feeling that completely empty, when just the thought of walking to the kitchen sink for a glass of water feels like you're trying to climb a mountain in a snowstorm, your perception of everything gets so terribly muddled. Were they louder? Were they quieter? Did they change their cadence? I'm simply not sure. I just know they didn't leave. They were still there in the walls, still murmuring about the archive and the museum board, but whether the pitch or the volume shifted... it's all just a heavy blur to me. 

It's a bit like asking if the rain sounds different against the glass when you're weeping, you know? You don't analyze the acoustics, you just know that it's still raining. So, no, I really couldn't say if they quieted down or got louder. I just didn't have the mental capacity to notice those kinds of fine details when I was feeling so utterly disconnected from the rest of the world. I just knew I was trapped in that chair, and they were still talking.

doctor.question: When you're feeling that heavy, gray emptiness and sitting in your armchair—during those deeply depressed periods—are you still absolutely convinced that the museum board is monitoring your telephone and tracking your work, or does that certainty fade away even though the voices might still be there?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I am convinced the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone because they know my Caribbean archive will change how the galleries tell the truth, and no one has shown me anything that proves otherwise.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my certainty about the museum board monitoring my telephone and tracking my work persists during depressed periods, which directly refers to my delusions.

patient.answer:
Oh, it doesn't fade. No, not in the slightest, Doctor. Even when I am sitting there, feeling like I have lead weights in my pockets and I can barely lift my head off the velvet cushion of that armchair... the certainty doesn't go anywhere. Because, you see, the facts don't change just because my mood has plummeted and I'm too exhausted to move. 

I am completely, absolutely convinced that the museum board—and, actually, the city arts people as well, they are definitely involved now—they have been monitoring my phone this entire time. Even when I'm not making calls! I sit there in the terrible grayness, staring at the drawer where I've wrapped the receiver in my scarves, and I know they're on the other end, just waiting, listening to the silence in my apartment. 

And why wouldn't they? They know exactly what I have sitting in those boxes. My Caribbean archive... it is so incredibly significant, Doctor. The way I've cataloged the photographs, the history from the islands, it is going to completely change how the galleries tell the truth. It will upend their entire curated narrative, and they are absolutely terrified of that. The city arts people are desperate to control the history, you see, to keep things exactly as they are. 

So, no, the conviction never leaves me. Not for a single second. People might try to dismiss it, but no one—absolutely no one—has shown me anything that proves otherwise. Not a single person has been able to give me a shred of evidence that my phone isn't tapped or that my archive isn't being watched. So I just sit there in the heavy stillness, watching the dead leaves on the rug, knowing that the moment I pick up that phone or touch a photograph from the Caribbean collection, they are logging it. You just can't turn off that kind of knowing, Doctor, no matter how terribly depressed you feel. It's exhausting, it really is, having to carry the immense weight of that truth while also feeling like you're drowning in a gray ocean... it just never stops.
